# Log odds, odds and odds ratios {#sec-regression-odds}

In the previous chapter, you encountered log odds in the context of Bernoulli regression model.
Log odds are the logarithm of the odds, as can be seen in the logit formula.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{logit}(p) & = ln(odds)\\
\text{odds} & = \frac{p}{1-p}
\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that the model estimates, derived from the MCMC posterior draws, are on the log-odds scale.
In the report of the model fitted in the previous chapter, we talked about differences in probability either as changes in percentage points or in log odds:

> At 80% probability, the probability of a multi-verb predicate decreases by 11-22 percentage points from home-signers to NSL1 ($\beta$ = -0.88 log odds, SD = 0.22), and increases by 25-36 points from NSL1 to NSL2 ($\beta$ = +0.56 log odds, SD = 0.21).

Something that we glossed over in the previous chapter is that the same change in log odds corresponds to a different change in percentage points depending on the baseline probability.
So for example a change in log odds of +1 corresponds to a change of about 23 percentage points when the baseline probability is 50% (approximately from 50% to 73%), but only about 3 percentage points when the baseline probability is 95% (approximately from 95% to 98%).
This is why it is useful to not only report changes in log odds, but also in percentage points.

## Odds ratios

Coefficients that indicate differences in log odds between two levels, like in the case of the NSL1 coefficient above $\beta = -0.88$, can also be expressed as odds ratios.
An **odds ratio (OR)** is the ratio of the odds of one level to the odds of the other level.
One can obtain odds ratios from log odds by exponentiating the log odds.

::: callout-tip
### Odds ratio

An **odds ratio** is the ratio between two odds and it is also the factor by which you multiply one odd to get the other.
:::

Let's go back to the model from @sec-regression-bernoulli.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
Warning: package 'Rcpp' was built under R version 4.6.1
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
library(posterior)

mvp_bm <- brm(
  Num_Predicates ~ Group,
  family = bernoulli,
  data = verb_org,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 1329,
  file = "cache/ch-regression-bernoulli_mvp_bm"
)
```
:::


We can extract the draws as usual and calculate the odd ratios for `NLS1` and `NLS2`.
We also calculate the 80% CrIs of the odds ratios.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Get draws
mvp_bm_draws <- as_draws_df(mvp_bm)

# Calculate posterior draws of odds ratios
mvp_bm_draws <- mvp_bm_draws |> 
  mutate(
    NSL1_OR = exp(b_GroupNSL1),
    NSL2_OR = exp(b_GroupNSL2),
  )

quantile2(mvp_bm_draws$NSL1_OR, c(0.1, 0.9)) |> round(2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 q10  q90 
0.31 0.55 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
quantile2(mvp_bm_draws$NSL2_OR, c(0.1, 0.9)) |> round(2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 q10  q90 
1.35 2.29 
```


:::
:::


We could then report the results like this:

> At 80% probability, the odds of a multi-verb predicate change by a factor of 0.31--0.55 from home-signers to NSL1 ($\beta$ = -0.88 log odds, SD = 0.22), and change by a factor of 1.35--2.29 from NSL1 to NSL2 ($\beta$ = +0.56 log odds, SD = 0.21).

Alternatively, odds ratio can be expressed as percent decrease with $(1 - OR) * 100$ when $OR < 1$ and percent increase $(OR - 1) * 100$ when $OR > 1$:

> At 80% probability, the odds of a multi-verb predicate decreases by 45-69% from home-signers to NSL1 ($\beta$ = -0.88 log odds, SD = 0.22), and increase by 35-129% from NSL1 to NSL2 ($\beta$ = +0.56 log odds, SD = 0.21).

While it is useful to know about odds and odd ratios, I personally find talking about differences in percentage points more straightforward when dealing with the substantive interpretations of the results.
I suggest that you stick to percentage points when reporting models results, while you learn the ropes of Bayesian regression models.
